explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, the Philistines. The writer says war broke out with them at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). They've been a thorn in Israel's side for a long time, and here they come again. Some folks just keep showing up to the same party uninvited.

Not the Moabites this time, friend. The text says war broke out with the Philistines at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). Moab is a neighbor of Israel, so I see how it slipped in. Still, the Philistines are the ones lining up on this battlefield.

Close neighbors, but not the ones at Gezer. The text says the war was with the Philistines (1 Chronicles 20:4). The Edomites don't show up anywhere in this passage. I once grabbed the wrong cookie cutter in the dark too, so no shame here.

True! Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). Sippai was a descendant of the Rephaim, a family known for big, big people. The text is plain about it: one man falls, and the battle turns.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai, a descendant of the Rephaim, at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). It sounded like a trick, I know. Sometimes the plain answer is just the plain answer.

Subdued is right. After Sippai was killed, the Philistines were subdued (1 Chronicles 20:4). That means they were brought low and their fight was held down. Think of dough after a good press, all the puff gone out of it.

Victorious would flip the whole story, friend. The text says the Philistines were subdued (1 Chronicles 20:4). Sippai fell, and Israel came out on top at Gezer. The Philistines don't get a victory lap here.
No rewards were handed out to the Philistines. The text says they were subdued (1 Chronicles 20:4). That's the opposite of getting a prize. Nobody walked away from Gezer with a gift basket.

Yes! Lahmi was the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5). Gittite means he was from Gath. Elhanan son of Jair is the one who killed Lahmi. That family name keeps turning up on the battlefield, and it never ends well for them.

Og was a giant king, so I see why you reached for him. He's the king of Bashan in Deuteronomy 3:11, though, and he isn't Lahmi's brother. The text says Lahmi was the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5). Big names in this crowd, friend, so it's easy to mix them up.

Sisera was a commander from the book of Judges (Judges 4:2), and he has nothing to do with this family. The text says Lahmi was the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5). Wrong battle, wrong century. I'd need a bigger apron to keep all these warriors straight.

explanations.answer: Six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot
explanations.explanation: That's it! The man had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (1 Chronicles 20:6). The text also says he was a man of great stature. Imagine trying to shake that hand. You'd need a second turn.

explanations.answer: A bronze coat of armor weighing five thousand shekels
explanations.explanation: That's Goliath's armor, friend. The text about him says the coat of mail weighed five thousand shekels of bronze (1 Samuel 17:5). The man at Gath is different. His thing was six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (1 Chronicles 20:6).

explanations.answer: An iron bed nine cubits long and four cubits wide
explanations.explanation: That bed belongs to Og king of Bashan, whose iron bed was nine cubits long and four cubits wide (Deuteronomy 3:11). Great pick for a big-person detail, but it's a different story. The man at Gath had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (1 Chronicles 20:6). Nobody mentions his furniture.

Twenty-four, that's it! Six fingers on each hand is twelve, and six toes on each foot is another twelve (1 Chronicles 20:6). Add them up and the text says "twenty-four in all." Good math, friend. I only count to ten on my own, and I have to borrow the mustache for the rest.

Close, but two short. Six fingers on each hand is twelve, and six toes on each foot is twelve more. The text says "twenty-four in all." (1 Chronicles 20:6) Good guess, friend, and easy to be off by a little.

A little too generous, friend. Six fingers on each hand is twelve, and six toes on each foot is twelve more. The text says "twenty-four in all." (1 Chronicles 20:6) Two extra digits would've been a lot even for this guy.

Yes! When the man at Gath taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei killed him (1 Chronicles 20:7). Shimei was David's brother, so Jonathan is David's nephew. A family member took care of it, and that's the whole story.

Abishai, Zeruiah's son, was one of David's fighting men, so I see why you picked him. He killed three hundred men with his spear in 1 Chronicles 11:20. At Gath, though, it was Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei who killed the man (1 Chronicles 20:7).

Benaiah, Jehoiada's son, is another of David's mighty men, and a strong pick. He's known for killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day (1 Chronicles 11:22). The man who taunted Israel at Gath fell to Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei (1 Chronicles 20:7).

David is right. The text says these descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). He's the king of Israel, and the battles all happen under his leadership. Several fighters did the work, and David's name is the one on the box.

Servants, yes. The text says they fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). That includes Sibbecai, Elhanan and Jonathan from this very passage. The king got the credit, and his team did the swinging.
Saul was Israel's first king, before David. He's not in this passage. The text says they fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). Saul's chapter was over by then, friend.

No priests here, friend. The text says the descendants of Rapha fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). The fighters named in this passage are warriors, and one is David's own nephew. The priests were handling other business.

Joab was David's army commander, so he's a good guess. He's the one who led the attack on Rabbah in 1 Chronicles 20:1. In verse 8, though, the text says they fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). Joab's name isn't in that line.
